cues.text: A Name Earned by Generosity

Born Joseph , a Levite of Jewish parentage on the island of Cyprus, Barnabas appears early in the Acts of the Apostles among the first generation of believers in Jerusalem who held all things in common.
He sold a field he owned and laid the proceeds at the Apostles' feet for distribution to the needy.
The Apostles themselves gave him a new name in recognition of this generosity and of the warmth of spirit that evidently accompanied it: Barnabas , traditionally rendered "son of encouragement."
It was a name that would prove, across the whole of his subsequent life, to be less a nickname than a vocation.
Vouching for a Former Persecutor
When Saul of Tarsus , the Church's most feared persecutor, arrived in Jerusalem after his own dramatic conversion.
The disciples there, understandably wary of a man whose reputation for violence against Christians was well known, refused to receive him.
Then Barnabas, alone among them, took Saul by the hand, brought him before the Apostles, and testified to what he had learned of Saul's genuine encounter with the Lord on the road to Damascus.
Without this single act of trust, extended to a man everyone else had every reason to fear, the Church's history might have unfolded very differently.

Barnabas's willingness to see past a fearsome reputation to the grace already at work beneath it opened the door through which the Apostle Paul would eventually walk into the whole of his later ministry.
Partners in the Gospel
Some years later, when the Church at Antioch experienced a great awakening of Gentile converts, the Jerusalem community sent Barnabas to investigate and encourage the new believers there.
Recognizing that the work had grown beyond what he alone could manage, Barnabas traveled to Tarsus to seek out Saul, who had spent the intervening years in relative obscurity.
He brought him back to Antioch, where the two labored together for a full year, teaching a congregation so vibrant that it was there believers were first called Christians .
When the Holy Spirit set the two apart for a wider mission, it was Barnabas and Saul together who set out from Antioch on what the Church remembers as the first great missionary journey.
Barnabas was named first, still evidently the senior figure at this stage.
They carried the Gospel across Cyprus and into the interior of Asia Minor.
A Voice for the Gentiles at Jerusalem
When controversy arose over whether Gentile converts needed to observe the full Mosaic Law, Barnabas and Paul returned to Jerusalem to lay the matter before the Apostles and elders.
The gathering became known as the Council of Jerusalem .
They recounted before the assembly the signs and wonders God had worked through them among the Gentiles.
This testimony helped secure the council's landmark decision not to burden Gentile believers with the full weight of Jewish ceremonial law.
The ruling confirmed that Gentile believers were not required to undertake the full Mosaic observance.
A Painful Parting, and a Quiet Legacy

Barnabas's steady generosity was tested once more when he and Paul prepared for a second missionary journey and disagreed sharply over whether to bring along Barnabas's young cousin, John Mark , who had abandoned the first journey partway through.

Paul judged the young man unreliable; Barnabas, true to the very name the Apostles had given him, refused to give up on him, and the two great missionaries parted ways, Barnabas taking Mark with him back to Cyprus.
That quiet, unglamorous act of continued encouragement bore fruit far beyond what either man could have foreseen.
The very Mark whom Paul had once distrusted would go on to become a faithful companion of Peter and the author of the Gospel that bears his name.
Barnabas's continued confidence in Mark may well have contributed to that development.
Legacy
Tradition holds that Barnabas continued preaching in his native Cyprus, where he was eventually martyred, and the island has honored him ever since as its founding apostle and patron.
Though overshadowed in later memory by the towering figure of his one-time companion Paul, Barnabas remains, in the Church's own earliest testimony, an apostle in every sense that mattered.
His particular gift was neither eloquence nor learning but simple, persistent encouragement, extended first to a feared persecutor and later to a discouraged young man.
He teaches every believer since that the quiet ministry of believing in someone else's unfinished potential can shape the future of the whole Church.
